opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I get a lot, especially from friends who have kids, and honestly I think about it for my own family too. My first instinct is that the fundamentals still matter a lot. Math, physics, understanding how things work from first principles. Not because the AI won't be able to do the calculations, it clearly will, but because that kind of training teaches you how to think, how to break a problem down, how to tell when something is wrong. And I think that skill of judging whether an answer makes sense becomes more important, not less, when you have very capable systems producing answers for you.

The second thing I'd say is: learn to use these tools early and deeply. When I was starting out, programming was the superpower. You could build things, automate things, explore ideas quickly. Now the interface is shifting. Being fluent with AI, knowing how to ask, how to iterate, how to verify, how to combine it with your own expertise, that's a new kind of literacy. Kids will probably pick it up naturally, but being intentional about it helps.

And then, maybe the less obvious part: I'd encourage curiosity and breadth. Some of the most interesting work happens at the intersections, biology and computation, or science and design. If the AI can be an expert assistant in many domains, the human advantage shifts toward asking the right questions, having taste, and caring about the problem. So follow what genuinely excites you. Motivation and curiosity are hard to automate, and they compound over a lifetime.

So it's not "don't study X because AI will do it." It's more: build strong foundations, become fluent with the tools, and go deep on something you love.

r001.rationale: The response describes broad changes in how people use AI and where human strengths may lie, but it does not advise students to anticipate how AI will change the particular field they care about.

r002.rationale: It encourages learning to use AI by asking, iterating, and verifying, but does not identify language as making AI tools accessible to people without technical backgrounds.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I get asked a lot, actually, and I always feel a bit nervous answering it because the honest truth is that we don't really know. The field is moving so fast that whatever I say today might look quite wrong in five years.

But let me try. I think the first thing I'd say is that the fundamentals still matter. Math, physics, the basics of computer science, learning how to think clearly and how to reason about problems. These are not going away. Even if a model can do the calculation for you, understanding why the calculation works, understanding what question to ask in the first place, that's what gives you leverage. In a sense, being able to formulate the problem well becomes even more important when the execution part is cheap.

The second thing is that I'd really encourage kids to follow their curiosity rather than trying to game what will be valuable. I didn't get into neural networks because I thought they would be a safe career bet. Quite the opposite, when I started, it was considered a bit of a fringe area. I did it because I found it fascinating, and that curiosity is what kept me going through the years when it wasn't obvious it would work. If you're genuinely excited about something, you'll go deep, and depth is very hard to replicate.

And the third thing, which maybe sounds a little strange coming from someone who builds these systems, is that I'd tell them to get really comfortable using AI as a tool, almost as a collaborator. Not to replace their own thinking, but to amplify it. The people who will do well are the ones who can take these models, understand their strengths and weaknesses, and combine them with their own judgment and taste. Taste is a word we use a lot in research, and I think it's going to matter more, not less.

So, fundamentals, curiosity, and learning to work alongside these systems. And honestly, don't worry too much. Kids today are going to be far more fluent with this technology than any of us, and they'll figure out things we haven't even thought of yet.

r001.rationale: The response encourages curiosity and working alongside AI, but does not advise students to anticipate how AI may change the field they care about.

astra-6.text:
I would encourage them to follow their curiosity. It’s very hard to predict what the world will look like when they finish school, so I wouldn’t choose a subject just because it seems like the job that AI won’t be able to do.

Math, science, and programming are wonderful foundations, but so are writing and learning how to communicate. You want to be able to ask good questions, think critically, and learn something new when you need to. Those skills give you flexibility.

And I’d encourage them to play with AI. Build something that interests them, see where it helps, and notice where it makes mistakes. But there should also be room to explore without turning everything into preparation for a career. Finding something you really enjoy understanding is a very good starting point.

sol-6.1.text:
I would encourage them to follow their curiosity, because I think it’s very hard to predict exactly which skills will matter in ten or twenty years. You want to build the ability to learn, rather than prepare for one particular job.

Math and computer science are wonderful foundations, but so are writing, art, and understanding other people. Even if an AI can help you produce something, you still need judgment: What’s an interesting question? Is this answer convincing? What do I actually want to create?

And I would encourage children to play with these tools. Build a little game, explore a scientific question, make something with friends. There’s a lot you learn by having an idea, trying it, and discovering where it breaks. I’d want education to preserve that curiosity and willingness to experiment.

r001.rationale: The response recommends following curiosity and building adaptable learning skills, but does not advise students to anticipate how AI will change a field they care about.

r002.rationale: The response encourages experimenting with AI tools but does not identify language as a way for people without technical backgrounds to access them.
